author: Mercury
text: 8h Mercury’s most popular Slack user is not an employee at all – it’s Hermes, our AI data bot that answers hundreds of questions a week from employees across the company. Employees are asking it things like: who are our customers? What percent of overall card spend is on agent cards? What are the most visited pages of the website, and how has that changed over the past six months? Hermes started as a Hack Week project, and getting it up and running happened quickly. Someone asks a data question in natural language in Slack, and underneath the Slack interface is a semantic layer, essentially a shared recipe book for Mercury's metrics. It tells Hermes how the company defines things, which data sources to use, and how different pieces of information fit together. The harder parts of maintaining Hermes are building our data for agents and continually updating the data foundation. What an agent wants from a data warehouse and data platform is radically different from what a human needs. Humans can remember rules and understand nuance a lot better than an agent can. Agents need guidelines and rules, or they pick randomly from multiple reasonable options. Every question became signal: what people needed, what they didn't understand, where the model was weak, and which parts needed to get better. author: drmaryclaire
text:
My mama, Mary Landry Pastor, passed away peacefully yesterday, surrounded by her family. She was 90.

Most of you knew her as Maugie; her grandchildren called her Gigi. She raised eight of us, and she ran the front of house in our family’s restaurants while Dad ran the back, which meant she was the first face everyone saw when they walked in the door. She outlived my dad and three of her sons (Jep, Bob, and Jude), and she kept going anyway, kept writing in her journals, kept loving the rest of us with everything she had.

I want to thank my brothers and sister, Jim, Leah, Jeremiah, and John. They were her caregivers, and they fought to make sure she had excellent care at the end of her life. That fight is the reason her last days were peaceful, and I’ll never be able to thank them enough. Thank you, too, to Janet and Claudette, who kept showing up for her, and to everyone who cared for her

I got fired 3x in a row for being "lazy."

6 years after the third firing, I was the CRO at one of the fastest-growing healthtech companies in the US.

After building that company to a valuation of over $1B, I quit and went all in on myself.

That silly little one-person business went on to create more than $15M in profit over 7 years.
